title: Stadium Gate Tallies
story: A stadium counts fans at its north and south gates with old counters that store a number as a chain of digits, ones digit first. So 4,071 fans is stored as 1 → 7 → 0 → 4. The counters were built to grow without limit, so a tally can be far longer than any built-in integer type can hold.
At the end of the night the stadium needs the total for both gates, stored the same way.
task: Write addTallies(north, south). Each argument is a non-empty linked list of digits (0 to 9), ones digit first. Return a linked list holding the sum, in the same format.
The lists may have different lengths. Neither has extra zeros at the end of the chain (its highest digit), except the number 0 itself, which is [0]. The result must follow the same rule.
constraints: Numbers can have up to 100 digits, so do not convert them to built-in numbers.

examples.explanation: That is 4,071 + 659 = 4,730. Ones: 1 + 9 = 10, write 0 carry 1. Tens: 7 + 5 + 1 = 13, write 3 carry 1. Hundreds: 0 + 6 + 1 = 7. Thousands: 4. Read ones first: 0, 3, 7, 4.
98 + 4 = 102. 8 + 4 = 12, write 2 carry 1. 9 + 1 = 10, write 0 carry 1. Both lists are finished but a carry is left, so it becomes a new digit, 1.

hints: Add 98 + 4 on paper. Which digit do you start with, and which way do you move?
Paper addition starts at the ones and moves left, passing a carry along. The lists are stored ones digit first, so walking the chain forwards is exactly the paper order.
At each position you add three things: a digit from each list (or 0 if that list has run out) and the carry. What happens when both lists end but the carry is still 1?

Walk both lists together with a carry starting at 0. While either list has nodes or carry is not 0: sum = digitA + digitB + carry, append a node with sum % 10, set carry = floor(sum / 10). Build the result with a dummy head and a tail pointer.
bruteForce: Turn each chain into a number, add the two numbers, and turn the result back into a chain.

That breaks as soon as a tally passes about 16 digits: JavaScript numbers lose precision beyond 9,007,199,254,740,991, and many languages overflow at 64 bits. With up to 100 digits the answer would be wrong. Python's integers grow without limit, so there it happens to work, but it skips the skill this problem is about. Adding digit by digit works for any length, in any language.

walkthrough: Storing the ones digit first is a gift: walking the chain forwards is the same order you use for addition on paper. So you just do paper addition, one node at a time, carrying as you go.
• The south list is done, so its digit counts as 0. 4 + 0 + 0 = 4. Write 4.
• Both lists are done and the carry is 0. Stop. Result: 0 → 3 → 7 → 4, which is 4,730.
The loop condition includes carry. Without it, 98 + 4 would stop at 2 → 0 and lose the final 1. That missing last carry is the classic bug in this problem.
solution.timeWhy: n and m are the two list lengths. One step per digit of the longer number, plus at most one extra step for the last carry.
solution.spaceWhy: The result has one node per digit. Apart from that, only a few variables.
solution.takeaway: When numbers are too big for built-in types, do the arithmetic the way you would on paper, digit by digit with a carry. Walking two lists of different lengths together, treating a finished list as zeros, is a pattern that comes back often.
